label: The Americas
subtitle: North, Central & South America, Caribbean
about: Cuisines of North, Central and South America and the Caribbean.

label: United States
subtitle: Regional, immigrant, Indigenous, diverse
about: The United States stretches from Atlantic and Gulf coasts through the Great Plains and Rockies to the Pacific, with Alaska and Hawai‘i adding still more distinct foodways. Native peoples, enslaved Africans, European colonists and successive migrations from Latin America, Asia and elsewhere shaped a highly regional cuisine; industrial food and restaurant culture later created national forms. Representative dishes include barbecue, fried chicken, clam chowder and hamburgers, but no seasoning set represents all US home cooking.
signature_ingredients: regional smoked meats (substitute: supermarket smoked sausage or bacon when appropriate)
hominy/grits (substitute: polenta only for texture, not exact flavor)
regional chile products (substitute: closest available chile)
tips: Commercial barbecue rub: often salt, sugar, paprika, chile, garlic and onion; replace an equal weight of recipe dry rub and reduce added salt (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium) from the label. Commercial poultry/seasoned-salt blends vary too much for a national rule; use 1:1 by weight only after checking sodium and ingredient order.
pitfalls: Do not equate US cuisine with fast food or with one Southern/Tex-Mex profile.
'American' restaurant exports overrepresent burgers, pizza, fried chicken, barbecue and sweet sauces, while home cooking is far more regional and immigrant-shaped.

label: Any
subtitle: Burgers, barbecue, fried chicken
about: Outside the United States, 'American food' is often pictured through nationally exported restaurant and media forms rather than regional home cooking: burgers, hot dogs, pizza, barbecue, fried chicken, steaks and diner-style comfort food. That image grew alongside mass production, fast-food systems and postwar restaurant culture, but it is a cliché of a much more diverse country. Representative export-image dishes include hamburgers, hot dogs, barbecue ribs and fried chicken.
signature_ingredients: American-style processed cheese (substitute: mild cheddar plus Monterey Jack)
liquid smoke (substitute: smoked paprika for aroma only, not true smoke)
cornmeal grits (substitute: coarse polenta)
tips: Bottled barbecue sauce can replace a homemade sweet-tart barbecue glaze 1:1 by weight, but reduce added sugar, vinegar and salt after tasting. Burger/grill seasoning blends can replace combined salt/spices 1:1 by weight; derive salt from sodium on the label.
pitfalls: Treat this as the international export stereotype, not a claim about what Americans usually cook at home.
Do not force Old Bay, ranch, maple syrup or bacon into unrelated dishes merely because they read as 'American.' Pizza in this node means Americanized pizza styles, not Italian cuisine.

label: New Mexican
subtitle: Red and green chile, blue corn
about: Centered along the high-desert Rio Grande corridor and Sangre de Cristo foothills, from Hatch and Las Cruces in southern New Mexico through Albuquerque, Santa Fe, and Chimayó in the north, New Mexican cuisine grew out of Pueblo, Navajo, and Apache farming fused with 16th–17th-century Spanish colonial traditions in long isolation from central Mexico, later absorbing ranching and Route 66 diner culture. Its cooking revolves around clean, un-smoked sauces made from flame-roasted green or sun-dried red New Mexico Capsicum annuum chiles, paired with pinto beans, blue corn, and wheat-flour tortillas or sopapillas. Representative dishes include carne adovada, stacked red/green/'Christmas' enchiladas, green chile stew, and posole.
flavors: roasted green New Mexico chile (chile verde de Nuevo México)
sun-dried red New Mexico chile (chile rojo / Chimayó)
crushed red New Mexico chile flakes (chile caribe)
signature_ingredients: flame-roasted New Mexico green chile (substitute: canned diced green chiles, drained with salt reduced, or roasted Anaheim chiles plus a small serrano)
dried New Mexico / Chimayó red chile pods (substitute: dried New Mexico or guajillo pods blended with a small pinch of pasilla)
blue cornmeal / masa (harina de maíz azul) (substitute: yellow or white masa harina or stone-ground cornmeal; loses blue corn's nutty aroma)
dried or frozen un-popped white hominy (posole) (substitute: drained canned white or golden hominy; softer texture and faster cooking)
New Mexican piñon pine nuts (substitute: Mediterranean pignoli pine nuts, milder and less resinous)
wild lamb's quarters greens (quelites) (substitute: fresh spinach or Swiss chard)
tips: Canned fire-roasted diced green chiles supply about 1.0 to 1.1 g salt per 113 g (4 oz) can, whereas plain flash-frozen roasted green chile is typically unsalted; check the package before reducing salt.
Canned red chile sauce supplies about 2.3 g salt per 240 g cup, and jarred green chile sauce averages about 3.4 g salt per 240 g cup; reduce recipe salt accordingly.
Pure ground New Mexico red chile powder contains 0 g salt, whereas generic US chili powder mixes cumin, oregano, garlic and salt and alters authentic New Mexican red chile flavor.
pitfalls: Do not confuse New Mexican cooking with Tex-Mex: keep red and green chile sauces clean with chile, garlic and oregano rather than heavy cumin or commercial chili-powder blends, and favor stacked corn enchiladas and sopaipillas.
Do not swap tomatillo salsa verde for roasted New Mexico green chile sauce or default to black beans instead of pinto or bolita beans.
Use 'Christmas' to mean half red and half green chile sauce on the plate, not a December holiday dish, and avoid smoky chipotle in classic sun-dried red chile sauces.
pantry: frozen roasted New Mexico green chile
pure ground New Mexico red chile or dried pods

label: Hawaiian & Local
subtitle: Shoyu, poke, kālua, local plates
about: Across the Hawaiian islands, culinary life spans two distinct layers: contemporary Hawaii island 'local food' forged in 19th- and 20th-century plantation camps and diners, and Indigenous Native Hawaiian (Kānaka ʻŌiwi) foodways built on taro (kalo), sweet potato, breadfruit, reef fish, and imu earth-oven roasting. ChefBot defaults to everyday Hawaii local food (blending Native Hawaiian staples with Japanese, Chinese, Filipino, Korean, and Portuguese influences alongside island pantry classics) while clearly naming Native Hawaiian dishes when making Indigenous heritage food. Representative dishes include shoyu or ʻinamona poke, kālua pork, laulau, loco moco, saimin, and two-scoop rice-and-mac-salad plate lunches.
flavors: Filipino fish sauce or shrimp paste (patis / bagoong)
sweet_only: coconut milk (waiū niu, mainly sweets like haupia and kūlolo)
dried salted plum powder (li hing mui)
roasted soy flour & red bean paste (kinako & azuki)
signature_ingredients: kalo taro corm, poi & lūʻau taro leaves (substitute: fresh taro root for boiled kalo; simmered baby spinach or collard greens for lūʻau leaves; no supermarket substitute for poi)
limu kohu / fresh ogo seaweed (substitute: plain unseasoned wakame or hijiki; softer texture and milder flavor)
ʻinamona roasted kukui nut (substitute: finely chopped toasted macadamia nuts mixed with flaky sea salt; note tree-nut allergy)
sashimi-grade ʻahi tuna or tako octopus (substitute: sushi-grade ahi tuna or wild salmon)
Hawaii-style Portuguese sausage (substitute: Portuguese linguiça or Spanish chorizo, usually less smoky)
ti leaves (kī) (substitute: banana leaves or parchment paper wrapped in heavy foil)
saimin noodles & dried shrimp dashi (substitute: thin crinkled ramen noodles without the packet, plus dashi from dried shrimp and kombu)
tips: Hawaii-brewed shoyu is slightly milder and about 15 to 20% less salty than standard Japanese soy sauce (about 2.0 g salt per 15 ml tbsp vs. 2.4 g): add a touch of extra salt or a tiny pinch of sugar if swapping standard soy sauce.
Packaged Hawaiian poke seasoning mixes (about 11 g per 450 g fish) supply around 6.7 g salt per packet: omit added paʻakai and reduce shōyu when using one.
Packaged smoke-salt kālua seasoning mixes run about 63% salt by weight (roughly 1.6 g mix per 1 g table salt omitted), and packaged char siu mixes supply roughly 7.2 g salt per 71 g packet.
Standard Cantonese-style oyster sauce supplies about 2.2 g salt per 15 ml tbsp.
pitfalls: Skip the pineapple-on-everything tourist cliché: canned pineapple chunks or juice in savory chicken, burgers or poke is export marketing, not Native Hawaiian or everyday local cooking.
Keep Indigenous Native Hawaiian dishes (poi, kalo, laulau, kālua pork) clearly distinguished from plantation-era multiethnic local food (Spam musubi, loco moco, plate lunches).
Let traditional poke highlight fresh fish, shōyu, toasted sesame oil, ogo, Maui onion and ʻinamona over plain rice rather than burying it under mayo sauces and unrelated toppings.
Traditional Hawaiian and local savory dishes rarely use coconut milk; cook kalo thoroughly and roast kukui nuts completely.

label: Native American
subtitle: Three Sisters, wild rice, cedar smoke
about: Spanning the Great Lakes waterways, Eastern Woodlands, Great Plains, arid mesas and Rio Grande valleys of the Southwest, and the cedar-lined Pacific Northwest coast, Native American foodways reflect hundreds of sovereign Indigenous nations connected by ancient trade networks such as Plains bison exchanges and coastal grease trails. Pre-colonial traditions center on seasonal hunting, fishing, foraging, and Three Sisters agriculture (corn, beans, and squash), kept distinct from post-1860s forced-relocation and reservation commodity foods like frybread made from government rations of white flour and lard. Representative regional dishes include Haudenosaunee white corn hominy soup, Anishinaabe manoomin (wild rice) broth and cakes, Pacific Northwest cedar-planked salmon, Diné juniper-ash blue corn mush, and Cherokee hickory-nut kanuchi.
flavors: staghorn or three-leaf sumac (Ojibwe: baakwaanaatig, Navajo: chííłchin, tart crimson berry seasoning)
juniper berries and juniper ash (Navajo: gad bi łeeshtʼiizh, resinous spice and alkaline nixtamalizing ash)
wild bergamot / bee balm (Lakota: waȟpé waštémna, Ojibwe: zaasab, oregano-mint aromatic leaf)
ramps / wild leeks and wild onions (Ojibwe: zhigaagawanzh, Mohawk: jion’kwasa)
native red and green chiles (Navajo: azeedíchʼííʼ, including New Mexico pods and chiltepín)
western red or northern white cedar (Ojibwe: giizhik, aromatic boughs and wood for planking, smoking, and mild infusions)
maple sugar and dark maple syrup (Ojibwe: ziinzibaakwad, used sparingly in savory glazes and squash)
hardwood culinary ash (Mohawk: onónhtara, mineral-rich alkaline agent for hominy)
spicebush berries and wild sage (Cherokee: nogatatli, warm citrus-allspice berry and resinous prairie or white sage)
sweet_only: sweetgrass (Ojibwe: wiingashk, vanilla-like aromatic grass used mainly in sweet infusions and syrups)
sweetened wild berry sauces such as chokecherry or blueberry wojapi (though tart unsweetened versions also accompany savory meats)
mesquite pod flour (caramel-toned native desert flour used mainly in contemporary Indigenous baking and puddings)
signature_ingredients: hand-harvested lake wild rice / manoomin (substitute: cultivated paddy wild rice, darker and firmer with a longer simmer time)
nixtamalized flint white or blue corn hominy (substitute: canned white or golden hominy, rinsed and drained, or masa harina for doughs)
tepary beans (substitute: dried pinto, navy, or black-eyed peas, which cook faster and are less earthy)
bison or venison (substitute: extra-lean grass-fed beef chuck or ground sirloin)
wild Pacific salmon, especially chinook or sockeye (substitute: farmed Atlantic salmon or steelhead trout, milder and higher in fat)
camas bulbs (substitute: none; slow-roasted sunchokes or sweet potatoes approximate the caramelized sweetness only loosely)
eulachon / oolichan grease (substitute: none; rendered duck fat or sunflower oil supplies cooking fat without the fermented marine depth)
hickory nuts for kanuchi (substitute: raw pecans mixed with a small amount of black walnuts)
prickly pear cactus pads and cholla buds (substitute: jarred nopales from Latin American markets, or green beans for crisp texture)
piñon pine nuts (substitute: mediterranean pine nuts, milder and less resinous)
tips: Canned white or golden hominy (standard 425 g / 15 oz can): usually contains nixtamalized corn, water, salt, and sometimes sodium bisulfite. Labels commonly list about 340 mg to 550 mg sodium per 1-cup serving (roughly 0.85 g to 1.4 g salt per cup, using about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium; uncertain across brands across manufacturers and rinsing). To replace dried hominy cooked from scratch (about 120 g dried yields 360 g cooked), drain and rinse canned hominy well and reduce added cooking salt by roughly 1 g to 2 g per can.

Jarred or canned red chile sauce (typically 425 g to 450 g jar): usually contains water, ground red chiles, tomato paste or vinegar, thickeners such as wheat or corn flour, garlic, spices, and salt. Sodium commonly falls around 200 mg to 370 mg per 60 mL to 120 mL serving (about 0.5 g to 0.9 g salt per serving, using about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium; uncertain across brands across regional styles). To swap from scratch, rehydrate and blend 30 g seeded dried red chiles with 250 mL unsalted broth or water and season separately.

Boxed long-grain and wild rice pilaf mix (typically 170 g dry package): usually combines white rice and small amounts of paddy wild rice with a seasoning packet of salt, hydrolyzed soy or corn protein, yeast extract, dried aromatics, and bouillon powder. Prepared servings often supply 640 mg to 740 mg sodium per 55 g dry portion (roughly 1.6 g to 1.85 g salt per serving, using about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium; uncertain across brands by package). To make from scratch, simmer 150 g pure wild rice in 600 mL unsalted stock with dried mushrooms, wild onion, and sage, omitting the packet.

Packaged frybread mix (post-reservation convenience product, typically 450 g to 900 g bag): usually contains enriched wheat flour, chemical leaveners (baking soda, monocalcium phosphate, or sodium acid pyrophosphate), cornstarch, sugar, and salt. Dry mix labels vary widely from roughly 350 mg to 790 mg sodium per 30 g to 40 g serving (about 0.9 g to 2.0 g salt per serving, using about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium; uncertain across brands across mixes). To make from scratch, whisk 240 g all-purpose wheat flour with 10 g baking powder and 3 g fine salt.

Bottled liquid smoke: pure wood-smoke concentrates usually contain only water and hickory, alder, or applewood smoke condensate with 0 mg sodium, whereas blended savory varieties often add vinegar, molasses, caramel color, salt, or soy-derived seasonings (commonly around 10 mg sodium per 5 mL teaspoon, negligible salt, though sauce-style blends vary; uncertain across brands across blended formulas). Use 2.5 mL to 5 mL per 1 kg braised meat or stew when wood-smoking or cedar-planking is unavailable.
pitfalls: Treating frybread, Indian tacos, or cheese-topped commodity dishes as pre-colonial cuisine rather than post-1860s reservation survival foods built from government rations of white flour and lard.
Flattening hundreds of distinct sovereign nations into one generic menu, such as putting Southwest chiles into Great Lakes wild rice soups or Pacific Northwest cedar-salmon dishes.
Confusing Indigenous North American corn-and-chile cooking with Tex-Mex restaurant fare by automatically adding ground cumin, cilantro, sour cream, and shredded cheddar cheese.
Thickening pre-colonial stews with European butter-and-wheat-flour roux or heavy cream instead of squash puree, parched cornmeal, or natural starch from steeping.
Assuming cultivated black paddy rice cooks like hand-harvested lake manoomin, which is lighter brown-green, nuttier, and cooks in roughly half the time.
pantry: nixtamalized cornmeal or masa harina (blue, white, or yellow)
dried heirloom beans (tepary, pinto, kidney, or cranberry)
sunflower oil or rendered duck or bison fat
pure maple syrup or maple sugar
dried red chiles or pure red chile powder
ground sumac and dried juniper berries

label: Pacific Northwest
subtitle: Cedar smoke, hazelnuts, shoyu, mushrooms
about: Stretching from the rocky Pacific coast, Puget Sound, and the Columbia River across the evergreen Cascade Mountains into the dry Columbia Basin, Washington and Oregon home cooking centers on cities such as Seattle and Portland alongside coastal fishing towns and inland orchard valleys. Rooted in Coast Salish, Chinook, and Plateau Indigenous First Foods—wild salmon, shellfish, camas, and native berries—and later shaped by Euro-American farmers, Nordic fishers, and Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, and Filipino immigrant communities along the Pacific Rim, everyday cooking favors lightly seasoned, ingredient-driven dishes. Representative home meals include cedar-plank or alder-smoked wild salmon, Seattle-style chicken teriyaki, pan-fried Pacific razor clams or creamy clam chowder, and Dungeness crab cakes or marionberry crisp.
flavors: Walla Walla sweet onion & green onion
miso paste (味噌, white or red miso)
toasted sesame oil (ごま油, goma abura)
dark-roast ground coffee or espresso (in savory dry rubs)
sweet_only: ground cinnamon (in apple, pear, and berry crisps)
ground cardamom (in Nordic-heritage sweet breads and buns)
signature_ingredients: wild Pacific salmon: Chinook/king, coho, or sockeye (substitute: frozen wild-caught Pacific salmon fillets; farmed Atlantic salmon is milder and fattier)
dungeness crab (substitute: lump blue crabmeat or snow crab legs, though Dungeness is sweeter and more tender)
pacific spot prawns (substitute: large shell-on wild pink or Gulf shrimp, cooked more briefly)
pacific oysters, Manila clams, or razor clams (substitute: east Coast littleneck clams or shucked oysters; no close supermarket substitute for razor clam tenderness)
geoduck clam (substitute: none for crisp sashimi siphon; chopped sea clams or squid for chowders)
wild chanterelle or morel mushrooms (substitute: cremini or oyster mushrooms, plus rehydrated dried wild mushrooms for aroma)
oregon hazelnuts / filberts (substitute: toasted blanched almonds or pecans, though hazelnuts have a distinct earthy flavor)
marionberries or trailing wild blackberries (substitute: standard cultivated blackberries with a splash of lemon juice or raspberry)
pacific Northwest orchard apples & pears such as Honeycrisp, Anjou, or Comice (substitute: firm crisp baking apples or ripe Bartlett or Bosc pears)
stinging nettles or fiddlehead ferns (substitute: baby spinach or Swiss chard for nettles; asparagus tips for fiddleheads)
tips: Bottled teriyaki sauce: usually contains soy sauce, sugar or corn syrup, vinegar or mirin, garlic, ginger, and starch thickeners. Standard ready-to-serve teriyaki sauce averages roughly 3,830 mg sodium per 100 g (about 690 mg sodium, or roughly 1.7 g salt at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium, per 18 g tablespoon; reduced-sodium styles vary widely (varies by brand)). Swap 18 g bottled glaze by combining 15 g regular soy sauce, 3 g brown sugar, and grated ginger and garlic, while omitting added table salt.

Commercial white or red miso paste: fermented soybeans, rice or barley koji, and salt, averaging about 3,730 mg sodium per 100 g (roughly 635 mg sodium, or about 1.6 g salt at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium, per 17 g tablespoon). White miso is typically milder (often 200 to 300 mg sodium, or 0.5 to 0.8 g salt, per 5 to 6 g teaspoon) while aged red miso often exceeds 300 to 400 mg sodium per teaspoon (uncertain across brands across brands and fermentation lengths). Reduce added table salt by roughly 1.5 g when stirring 17 g miso into broths, glazes, or compound butter.

Packaged alder-smoked seafood rub or cedar-plank seasoning blend: usually blends salt, brown sugar, paprika, garlic, onion, black pepper, and smoke flavoring or smoked salt. Sodium varies sharply by ratio of sugar to salt (commonly around 200 to 400 mg sodium, or roughly 0.5 to 1.0 g salt per teaspoon for sugar-herb rubs, versus about 280 to 420 mg sodium, or 0.7 to 1.05 g salt, per quarter teaspoon of pure alder-smoked flaky sea salt depending on crystal density (varies by brand)). Use weight-for-weight in place of plain dry herbs and sugar rubs, and withhold added salt until tasting.

Bottled sea clam juice: clam broth with added salt, usually around 410 to 465 mg sodium per 100 g (about 1.0 to 1.2 g salt per 100 g at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium, or roughly 2.5 to 2.9 g salt per 240 g cup; salted versus unsalted formulations vary (varies by brand)). Swap 1:1 by weight for homemade clam-steaming liquid in chowders and pan sauces, reducing added salt accordingly.
pitfalls: Confusing modern backyard cedar-plank grilling with historical Coast Salish cooking, which traditionally roasted split salmon upright on cedar or alder stakes angled around an open fire.
Treating every dish as fine-dining foraging while ignoring everyday home staples like Seattle-style chicken teriyaki, razor clam chowder, pan-fried oysters, and orchard fruit crisps.
Substituting farmed Atlantic salmon for wild Pacific Chinook, coho, or sockeye without adjusting cooking time, since wild Pacific salmon is leaner and dries out rapidly if overcooked.
Adding coffee or espresso indiscriminately to delicate crab or shellfish, when dark-roast coffee is usually reserved for meat dry rubs, chilis, and desserts.
Erasing the sharp divide between the wet maritime coast west of the Cascades and the dry eastern Columbia Basin and Yakima or Walla Walla valleys that supply sweet onions, apples, and grain.
pantry: neutral cooking oil and toasted sesame oil

label: Great Lakes
subtitle: Walleye, wild rice, rye, dill, dairy
about: Spanning Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan along Lakes Superior, Michigan, Huron, and Erie—from Minneapolis-St. Paul and Duluth to Green Bay, Milwaukee, Detroit, and the Upper Peninsula—this cuisine draws on glacial lakes, marshland wild rice beds, coastal cherry orchards, and dairy pastures. Shaped by Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) and Dakota fishing, foraging, and maple-sugaring alongside French-Canadian fur traders, Cornish miners, and Scandinavian, German, Polish, Finnish, and Belgian immigrants, everyday cooking usually balances sweet freshwater fish, winter preservation such as smoking, curing, and pickling, rye and caraway, sharp mustard, and farmstead butter and cheese. Representative dishes include pan-fried walleye or Friday fish fry yellow perch, smoked lake whitefish or Door County whitefish boil, wild rice soup or pilaf, and Upper Peninsula beef-and-rutabaga pasties.
flavors: fresh or dried dill (koper in Polish, tilli in Finnish)
caraway seed (Kummel in German, kminek in Polish)
brown, yellow, or horseradish mustard (Senf in German, musztarda in Polish)
prepared horseradish (Meerrettich in German, chrzan in Polish)
apple cider vinegar or distilled white vinegar
whole allspice and juniper berries (kryddpeppar and enbar in Swedish, used in Scandinavian curing and meatballs)
dried marjoram (majeranek in Polish, Majoran in German; signature herb of kielbasa and hearty stews)
pure maple syrup or maple sugar (zhiiwaagamizigan in Anishinaabemowin, used in savory glazes, curing brines, and Indigenous dishes)
lager or pilsner beer (cooking liquid for fish-fry batters, bratwurst braising, and beer-cheese soup)
sweet_only: ground cardamom (kardemumma, classic spice in Finnish pulla and Scandinavian sweet breads)
almond extract and almond paste (used in Danish-Wisconsin kringle, Scandinavian almond bars, and cherry tarts)
signature_ingredients: hand-harvested lake wild rice / manoomin (substitute: cultivated paddy wild rice, which is darker, firmer, and less nutty; avoid packaged rice pilaf mixes dominated by white rice)
walleye fillets (substitute: fresh yellow perch, sauger, or mild flaky haddock or pollock)
yellow perch fillets (substitute: walleye, freshwater trout, or small mild flounder or sole fillets)
fresh or hot-smoked lake whitefish (substitute: rainbow trout or Arctic char for fresh fillets; hot-smoked trout for smoked whitefish spread)
fresh squeaky cheddar cheese curds (substitute: young mild white cheddar cubed small, though it lacks the signature squeak and fried stretch)
wisconsin brick, Colby, or Limburger cheese (substitute: mild Muenster or young Havarti for brick; Monterey Jack-cheddar blend for Colby; washed-rind Munster for Limburger)
montmorency tart cherries, fresh, frozen, or water-packed (substitute: jarred sour Morello cherries; sweet Bing cherries with lemon juice do not match tart cherry acidity)
rutabaga / swede for Upper Peninsula pasties (substitute: turnip or parsnip; carrots alter classic Cornish-Yooper flavor and are debated locally)
coarse or dark rye flour (substitute: medium rye flour mixed with whole-wheat flour; all-purpose flour alone lacks the earthy tang of regional breads and fish coatings)
fresh Polish-style kielbasa or Wisconsin veal-and-pork bratwurst (substitute: unsmoked or lightly smoked pork garlic sausage; avoid sweet fennel Italian sausage)
tips: Commercial seasoned fish-fry breading or batter mix: typically wheat flour, cornmeal or cornstarch, leavening, onion and garlic powder, black pepper, paprika, and salt; dry mixes range roughly from 3,000 to 4,500 mg sodium per 100 g (about 7.5 to 11.3 g salt per 100 g at roughly 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium, or about 0.8 to 1.1 g salt per 10 g tablespoon, though amounts vary as salt varies widely by brand). Swap 1:1 by weight for homemade flour-and-cornmeal coating and omit added salt from the breading and fish.

Commercial chicken or beef bouillon cube or paste: contains dehydrated meat or vegetable extract, yeast extract or hydrolyzed protein, fat, aromatics, and salt; standard dry cubes average roughly 24,000 mg sodium per 100 g (around 1,150 mg sodium, or about 2.9 g salt, per 5 g cube at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium, though pastes and reduced-salt styles vary, approximate). Dissolve one 5 g cube in 240 g water to replace unsalted stock and reduce added recipe salt by roughly 2.5 to 3 g.

Jarred prepared horseradish: grated horseradish root, distilled vinegar, water, and salt (plus oil or cream in creamy versions); plain prepared horseradish averages roughly 420 mg sodium per 100 g (about 1.05 g salt per 100 g, or roughly 0.16 g salt per 15 g tablespoon at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium, though amounts vary across brands and creamy styles). Swap 1:1 by weight for freshly grated horseradish with a splash of white vinegar, adjusting dish salt lightly to taste.

Jarred tartar sauce: mayonnaise, diced dill pickles or sweet relish, onion or capers, dill, and salt; commercial jars typically carry around 600 to 700 mg sodium per 100 g (about 1.5 to 1.75 g salt per 100 g, or roughly 0.25 g salt per 15 g tablespoon at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium, though amounts vary across brands). Use 1:1 by weight as a ready condiment alongside fried perch or walleye in place of homemade mayonnaise-pickle-dill sauce.

Store-bought pickling spice blend: usually whole mustard seed, allspice, black peppercorn, coriander, bay leaf, clove, and dill seed with 0 g salt (though brine packets contain curing or pickling salt—check the label). Swap 1:1 by weight (about 2 g per teaspoon) for whole mixed pickling spices.
pitfalls: Reducing Upper Midwest and Great Lakes cooking to canned cream-of-mushroom soup casseroles while overlooking fresh lake fish, Indigenous wild rice (manoomin), scratch dairy, and cured European meats.
Treating industrially farmed paddy wild rice as identical to hand-harvested lake manoomin, which is usually lighter in color, nuttier, and quicker-cooking.
Substituting fennel-heavy sweet Italian sausage for warm-spiced Upper Peninsula cudighi (cinnamon, nutmeg, clove, red wine) or marjoram-and-garlic Polish kielbasa and Wisconsin bratwurst.
Presenting carrots versus rutabaga or gravy versus ketchup on Upper Peninsula Cornish pasties as a settled rule when local cooks actively dispute both.
Confusing Great Lakes freshwater fish fries (walleye, yellow perch, lake whitefish, bluegill) with coastal New England clam-and-haddock fries or Southern cornmeal catfish.
pantry: unsalted butter and neutral frying oil
apple cider vinegar or white vinegar

label: Appalachian
subtitle: Soup beans, sorghum, ramps, cornmeal
about: Spanning the Blue Ridge, Great Smoky, and Cumberland mountains across western North Carolina, eastern Tennessee, eastern Kentucky, West Virginia, and western Virginia, Appalachian cuisine grew out of forested coves, cold mountain streams, and small homesteads. It blends Cherokee and neighboring Indigenous agriculture and foraging (corn, heirloom beans, squash, ramps, and woodland greens) with Scots-Irish, English, and German preservation traditions, the skill of enslaved and free Black and Affrilachian cooks, and later coal- and timber-camp influences. Everyday mountain cooking favors slow-simmered dried beans and greens seasoned with cured pork, cast-iron cornmeal baking, orchard fruit, and spring wild foods, exemplified by soup beans with unsweetened cornbread, shucky beans (leather britches), buttermilk biscuits with sawmill gravy, apple stack cake, and pan-fried mountain trout.
flavors: garden sage (classic in fresh pork sausage and poultry dressing)
summer savory (traditional herb for green beans and poultry)
pepper vinegar (whole hot chiles steeped in vinegar)
chow-chow (pickled green-tomato, cabbage, and pepper relish)
mustard seed and celery seed (in chow-chow and slaws)
black coffee (deglazing liquid for country-ham red-eye gravy)
signature_ingredients: shucky beans / leather britches, air-dried whole green bean pods (substitute: none for the chewy dried-pod texture; dried pinto beans make a different soup-bean dish)
heirloom dried beans such as greasy, half-runner, or soup beans (substitute: dried pinto beans or Great Northern beans)
ramps / wild mountain leeks (substitute: scallions plus a small clove of garlic, milder)
sorghum syrup (substitute: light or mild cane molasses; sweeter and lacks sorghum's grassy tang)
country ham, dry salt-cured aged ham (substitute: prosciutto for sliced texture, or smoked ham with extra black pepper, though much milder)
fatback or cured salt pork (substitute: thick-cut unsmoked slab bacon, or smoked bacon if smokiness is acceptable)
dried apples (substitute: unsweetened dried apple rings rehydrated in apple cider or water)
morel mushrooms (substitute: dried or fresh cremini and shiitake mushrooms, less woodsy)
fresh mountain brook or rainbow trout (substitute: farmed rainbow trout or Arctic char)
cushaw squash (substitute: butternut squash or winter pumpkin)
tips: Commercial self-rising flour and self-rising cornmeal typically contain flour or cornmeal pre-blended with baking powder and salt, supplying roughly 1,000 to 1,350 mg sodium per 100 g (about 2.5 to 3.4 g salt per 100 g, calculated as about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium; uncertain across brands across brands, check the nutrition label). Swap 1:1 by weight for plain flour or cornmeal in biscuits and cornbread, omit separate baking powder, and subtract that label-derived salt from the recipe.

Commercial ham base or pork bouillon paste and cubes usually contain salt, cooked or smoked ham, pork stock, sugar, hydrolyzed soy or corn protein, and smoke flavoring, often supplying roughly 690 to 1,100 mg sodium per 4 to 6 g teaspoon or cube (about 1.7 to 2.8 g salt per teaspoon using about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium; uncertain across brands across brands). Dissolve 5 to 6 g in 240 g hot water to stand in for 240 g ham-bone broth in beans or greens, and withhold added salt until tasting.

Jarred chow-chow usually combines cabbage, green tomatoes, onions, peppers, vinegar, sugar, mustard seed, turmeric, and brining salt at roughly 190 to 600 mg sodium per 100 g (about 0.5 to 1.5 g salt per 100 g; uncertain across brands across brands); use 1:1 by weight as a table relish without extra salt.

Commercial apple butter is slow-cooked apples, cider, sugar, and warm spices with negligible sodium (typically under 3 mg per 15 to 18 g tablespoon); swap 1:1 by weight for homemade apple butter with no salt adjustment.
pitfalls: Do not sweeten savory Appalachian cornbread with sugar or default to cake-like yellow cornbread; traditional mountain versions usually rely on unsweetened stone-ground white cornmeal baked in hot fat-greased cast iron.
Do not collapse Appalachian cuisine into Deep South soul food or coastal Lowcountry cooking; okra, rice pilaus, shellfish, and heavy Cajun spice blends are not core Blue Ridge or Cumberland staples.
Do not treat sorghum syrup as identical to sugarcane molasses or corn syrup; sorghum comes from pressed sweet sorghum cane and has a distinct grassy, mildly tart finish.
Do not invent nostalgic pioneer clichés or suggest unsafe foraging such as eating raw or mature pokeweed, which must be harvested as young shoots and boiled in multiple changes of water.
Do not treat northern coal-camp specialties like West Virginia pepperoni rolls or Preston County buckwheat cakes as universal across the Blue Ridge, nor erase Cherokee and Affrilachian contributions.

label: Cajun
subtitle: Roux, trinity, smoke, cayenne
about: Cajun food is rooted in Acadiana, the bayous and prairies of southern Louisiana west and southwest of New Orleans. Acadian descendants mixed French traditions with Indigenous, African, Spanish, German and other local influences, using rice, pork, game and Gulf or swamp foods in practical country cooking. Gumbo, jambalaya, crawfish étouffée and boudin are representative; many, but not all, savory dishes begin with onion, celery and green bell pepper.
signature_ingredients: andouille sausage (substitute: smoked kielbasa plus extra black pepper/cayenne)
tasso (substitute: smoked ham)
crawfish (substitute: shrimp, though flavor changes)
tips: Use the separate spices in the recipe itself, never a store-bought blend. Then add a tip for cooks short on time: most Cajun seasoning is paprika, cayenne, garlic, onion, black pepper, oregano and thyme plus a lot of salt, so say how many grams of blend would replace the spices in this recipe, and to cut the added salt if they use it.

Never use or suggest filé powder. When a dish needs body (gumbo, étouffée), thicken it with okra, with a dark roux plus a reduced, collagen-rich homemade stock, or with xanthan gum weighed in grams (about 1 to 3 g per liter of liquid, blended in).

Jarred roux: typically flour cooked in fat; use roughly the same weight as finished roux called for, then thin into hot liquid. Cajun seasoning: often salt, paprika, cayenne, garlic/onion and herbs; replace the same weight of combined dry seasonings and reduce salt by about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium from the label.
pitfalls: Do not require a dark roux in every Cajun dish; étouffées, fricassées and gumbos vary, and some gumbos are thickened with okra.
Do not enforce 'Cajun never uses tomatoes': tomato use is less associated with classic Cajun than Creole cooking, but the rural/urban and tomato/no-tomato divide is an oversimplification.
Excessive cayenne is another stereotype; seasoning is often layered rather than simply hot.
pantry: onions, celery and green bell peppers (the trinity)

label: Creole
subtitle: Tomato, trinity, herbs, sauces
about: Louisiana Creole cooking is most strongly associated with New Orleans and the lower Mississippi River/Gulf world, though Creole identity also exists in rural Louisiana. It developed through French and Spanish colonial rule and the cooking knowledge of African and Afro-Creole people, with Caribbean, Native American, German, Italian and other influences. Shrimp Creole, gumbo, red beans and rice, grillades and jambalaya are representative, and restaurant, home and working-class Creole traditions are not identical.
signature_ingredients: creole mustard (substitute: Dijon plus a little whole-grain mustard)
andouille (substitute: smoked kielbasa)
tasso (substitute: smoked ham)
tips: Use the separate spices in the recipe itself, never a store-bought blend. Then add a tip for cooks short on time: most Creole seasoning is paprika, garlic, onion, cayenne, black and white pepper, oregano, thyme and basil plus a lot of salt, so say how many grams of blend would replace the spices in this recipe, and to cut the added salt if they use it.

Never use or suggest filé powder. When a dish needs body (gumbo, étouffée), thicken it with okra, with a dark roux plus a reduced, collagen-rich homemade stock, or with xanthan gum weighed in grams (about 1 to 3 g per liter of liquid, blended in).

Creole seasoning: usually salt, paprika, cayenne, garlic/onion and herbs; swap 1:1 by weight for the recipe's dry seasoning mix and reduce added salt from label sodium (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium). Bottled Creole mustard can replace prepared mustard 1:1 by weight but is sharper and grainier.
pitfalls: Do not define Creole as simply 'fancy Cajun' or claim it always uses cream, butter or tomatoes.
Historians emphasize overlap and continual change; New Orleans Creole cooking also includes Black working-class traditions.
Red jambalaya is common in New Orleans, but jambalaya exists in many forms, including brown versions.
pantry: onions, celery and green bell peppers (the trinity)

label: Southern & Soul
subtitle: Greens, corn, smoke, hot sauce
about: Southern food spans the Atlantic seaboard, Appalachia, the Deep South and Gulf states; soul food is a related African American tradition rooted especially in the South and carried nationwide during the Great Migrations. Indigenous crops and techniques, West and Central African knowledge, European settlement, enslavement and later migration all shaped these cuisines. Fried chicken, greens with potlikker, cornbread, Hoppin' John and barbecue are representative, but Southern food and soul food are overlapping rather than interchangeable.
signature_ingredients: stone-ground grits (substitute: coarse polenta, with flavor/texture loss)
country ham (substitute: prosciutto plus a little smoke, or smoked ham)
sorghum syrup (substitute: molasses, sweeter and stronger)
benne seeds (substitute: sesame seeds)
tips: Seasoned salt: replace the same weight of recipe salt-plus-spices, but calculate its salt from label sodium (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium). Bottled hot sauce can replace vinegar plus cayenne only approximately; start around 1:1 by weight with the vinegar component and reduce separately added cayenne to taste.
pitfalls: Do not reduce soul food to 'slave scraps' or portray it as uniformly unhealthy; scholarship documents skilled Black cooks, agriculture, entrepreneurship and celebration.
Do not merge all Southern barbecue into one sauce or meat style, and do not assume every Southern dish belongs specifically to soul food.

label: Tex-Mex
subtitle: Chile gravy, cumin, cheese, tortillas
about: Tex-Mex developed in Texas, especially San Antonio and South Texas, from long-standing Mexican and Tejano foodways interacting with Anglo-American commerce and later restaurant culture. It is a Mexican American regional cuisine, not a mistaken version of Mexican food. Chili con carne, cheese enchiladas with chile gravy, nachos, breakfast tacos and fajitas are representative.
signature_ingredients: yellow or processed melting cheese (substitute: mild cheddar plus Monterey Jack)
masa harina (substitute: fresh masa; no close wheat substitute)
dried ancho chiles (substitute: mild New Mexico dried chile)
Mexican chorizo (substitute: fresh pork sausage seasoned with chile, vinegar and garlic)
tips: Commercial chili powder: usually ground chile plus cumin, oregano, garlic and sometimes salt; replace the same weight of those dry spices, then adjust salt from sodium. Taco seasoning packets: often chile, cumin, garlic/onion, starch and substantial salt; use about 8–10 g per 450 g meat as a starting shortcut, varies widely because brands vary; subtract label-derived salt.
pitfalls: Do not 'correct' Tex-Mex into interior Mexican cuisine: yellow cheese, cumin-forward chile gravy, combination plates and crispy tacos have their own regional history.
Conversely, do not label every burrito, chimichanga or fish taco Tex-Mex; some were popularized in other US-Mexican regional traditions.

label: New England
subtitle: Salt pork, molasses, cider, cold sea
about: Stretching across the six northeastern states from Connecticut and Rhode Island up through Massachusetts, Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine, New England cooking spans cold Atlantic fishing ports, rocky inland farms, maple forests, and industrial mill cities. Shaped by Indigenous Wampanoag, Narragansett, and Abenaki foodways, English colonial thrift, Caribbean molasses trade, and later Irish, French-Canadian, Italian, and Azorean-Portuguese migrations, its everyday home cooking favors slow-simmered one-pot meals, plain dairy-and-pork-enriched seafood, and orchard or berry baking. Representative everyday dishes include New England clam or haddock chowder, Boston baked beans with steamed brown bread, New England boiled dinner, and SouthCoast Portuguese kale soup.
flavors: summer savory (for poultry, beans and chowder)
dark molasses (in savory baked beans and brown bread)
massa de pimenta (Azorean red pepper paste; southeastern Massachusetts and Rhode Island)
signature_ingredients: quahogs or chowder clams (substitute: finely chopped littleneck clams plus bottled clam juice; canned clams change the texture)
salt pork (substitute: thick-cut unsmoked slab bacon, or smoked bacon if a little smokiness is fine)
haddock or fresh Atlantic cod (substitute: pollock or Pacific cod)
salt cod, bacalhau (substitute: none for the cured texture; fresh cod makes a different dish)
Portuguese chouriço or linguiça (substitute: Spanish cured chorizo with extra garlic and paprika; the flavor differs)
stone-ground white flint cornmeal for Rhode Island jonnycakes (substitute: any stone-ground white or yellow cornmeal)
dark maple syrup (substitute: none for real maple flavor; dark brown sugar with molasses only approximates the sweetness)
fresh cranberries (substitute: frozen whole cranberries; dried ones only for baking or garnish)
tips: Store-bought poultry seasoning is usually salt-free sage, thyme, marjoram, rosemary, black pepper and sometimes ginger; it replaces the same dried herbs 1:1 by weight (about 1 g per teaspoon), with no salt change.

Jarred massa de pimenta is red peppers, coarse salt and often vinegar, roughly 12 to 13 g salt per 100 g (about 2 g per tablespoon; brands vary). Instead of 15 g paste, use 15 g minced sweet or mild chile plus 1.5 to 2 g salt, and taste before adding more salt.
Bottled clam juice is clam broth and salt, roughly 1 to 1.5 g salt per 240 g cup (brands vary); it replaces strained clam-steaming liquid 1:1 by weight, with less added salt.
Canned brown bread and canned baked beans come cooked with molasses and salt (the beans run roughly 1 to 1.3 g salt per 130 g serving); serve them as a side rather than as an ingredient swap.
pitfalls: Treating roadside tourist lobster rolls, fried whole-belly clams, and commercial clambakes as everyday home cooking.

Erasing the sharp north-south split: Vermont/Maine favor maple, wild blueberries, and French-Canadian dishes like tourtiere, whereas Massachusetts/Rhode Island lean toward molasses, clear RI chowder, jonnycakes, and Portuguese SouthCoast cooking.
Omitting Portuguese-American staples (chourico, linguica, massa de pimenta, caldo verde) in southeastern Massachusetts and Rhode Island.
Adding tomatoes to New England clam chowder (Manhattan style) or thickening chowder into a heavy library-paste roux instead of using potato starch and light cream or milk.
Repeating the exaggerated myth that colonial prisons routinely fed inmates lobster as cruel punishment.

label: Italian-American
subtitle: Slow red gravy, garlic, mozzarella, pork
about: Centered on New York City's five boroughs, Long Island, Westchester and the lower Hudson Valley, northern and central New Jersey, and Fairfield and New Haven counties in Connecticut, this regional American cuisine emerged when 1880-1924 immigrants—over 80 percent from Campania, Sicily, Calabria, Puglia, and Basilicata—adapted Southern Italian cooking to abundant American meat, dairy, and canned tomatoes. Shaped by neighborhood pork stores, salumerie, Italian bakeries, and multi-generational Sunday tables, it is a distinct American culinary tradition rather than a copy of food in modern Italy. Representative dishes include Sunday gravy with meatballs and braciole, chicken or eggplant parmigiana, baked ziti, sausage and peppers, the New York slice, New Haven white clam apizza, and the Christmas Eve Feast of the Seven Fishes.
flavors: garlic (aglio, often sliced thin and just golden in olive oil)
dried oregano (origano, on pizza, clam pies and baked dishes)
fennel seed (finocchio, the spice of Italian-American pork sausage)
dry red or white wine (vino rosso, vino bianco)
sweet_only: orange flower water (acqua di fiori d'arancio, in pastiera and ricotta fillings)
signature_ingredients: low-moisture whole-milk mozzarella (substitute: supermarket block low-moisture mozzarella; avoid fresh watery mozzarella on baked ziti or NY-style pizza)
whole-milk ricotta (substitute: supermarket whole-milk ricotta, drained in cheesecloth if watery)
hot or sweet capocollo / gabagool (substitute: cured coppa or thinly sliced spicy cured pork shoulder)
fresh sweet or hot fennel-spiced Italian pork sausage (substitute: bulk pork sausage seasoned with crushed fennel seed, garlic, and red pepper)
canned San Marzano-style whole peeled plum tomatoes (substitute: quality canned California whole peeled plum tomatoes)
escarole (substitute: chicory or sturdy curly endive; spinach changes bitterness and texture)
salt cod / baccala for Feast of the Seven Fishes (substitute: none for cured texture; fresh cod only for non-traditional swaps)
imported Pecorino Romano or aged Parmigiano-style cheese (substitute: aged domestic sheep's-milk pecorino or supermarket wedge Parmesan)
tips: Store-bought Italian seasoning is usually salt-free dried basil, oregano, rosemary, thyme and marjoram (check the label: some blends add salt); it replaces the same dried herbs 1:1 by weight, about 1.5 to 2 g per teaspoon.

Jarred marinara is tomatoes, olive oil, onion, garlic, herbs and salt, roughly 0.8 to 1.5 g salt per 100 g depending on the brand; it replaces crushed tomatoes plus aromatics 1:1 by weight, with about 1 g less added salt per 100 g of sauce.

Pre-grated shaker Parmesan or Romano has anti-caking cellulose and roughly 3.5 to 4.5 g salt per 100 g; it won't melt smoothly into a sauce, so use it only as a garnish, 1:1 by weight for freshly grated cheese.
pitfalls: Treating NYC-area Italian-American dishes (chicken parmigiana, baked ziti, Sunday gravy, pepperoni slices, the Feast of the Seven Fishes) either as inauthentic mistakes or as everyday food in Italy.
Using dialect spellings like 'gabagool', 'rigott' or 'pasta fazool' as shopping-list ingredients instead of standard grocery names.
Insisting on 'gravy' or 'sauce' as an absolute rule when local families themselves disagree.
Adding heavy cream to pasta sauces that rely on ricotta, pasta water, or slow-simmered tomato and pork fat, or putting fresh watery mozzarella on New York pizza and baked ziti.
Confusing cream-based fettuccine Alfredo (a wider American restaurant dish) with the region's pork-store and red-sauce cooking.
Confusing a New Haven plain tomato pie (no mozzarella by default) with a New York cheese slice.
pantry: canned whole or crushed plum tomatoes and tomato paste
dried oregano and red pepper flakes
a wedge of Pecorino Romano or Parmesan

label: Québécois
subtitle: Maple, summer savory, warm spices
about: Rooted along the St. Lawrence River valley, the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean basin, and the Appalachian foothills around Montreal and Quebec City, Québécois cuisine fuses 17th-century northwestern French settler cooking with Indigenous maple sugar making, British and Irish influences, and 20th-century Montreal traditions. Unlike classical French cooking with wine and cream reductions, traditional Quebec home kitchens rely on dry-toasted flour (farine grillée), summer savory, warm baking spices (clove, cinnamon, nutmeg, allspice), lard, maple, and molasses across hearty everyday dishes like soupe aux pois, pâté chinois, cretons, tourtière, and ragoût de boulettes, alongside seasonal sugar-shack fare (fèves au lard, oreilles de Christ / fried salt pork) and classic diner dishes like poutine.
flavors: yellow onion & celery (oignon jaune et céleri)
signature_ingredients: fresh unaged cheddar cheese curds (fromage en grains frais) (substitute: mild white cheddar cut into 2.5 cm chunks or fresh mozzarella pearls; loses the signature squeak)
dried whole or split yellow peas (pois jaunes) (substitute: dried yellow split peas)
cured salt pork / fatback (lard salé) (substitute: packaged US salt pork, or uncured pork belly / slab bacon with added salt reduced)
small white navy beans (haricots ronds blancs) (substitute: dried navy beans or Great Northern beans)
pork hocks / trotters (pattes de cochon) (substitute: fresh or smoked pork hocks)
Montreal smoked beef brisket (viande fumée de Montréal) (substitute: deli pastrami, though sweeter and less pepper-coriander crusted)
tips: Prepared poutine gravy mix pouches (around 52 g making 625 ml) supply roughly 8.7 g salt per pouch: if swapping in homemade beef-chicken stock thickened with cornstarch or toasted flour, add about 8 to 9 g salt per 625 ml batch.
Concentrated liquid beef broth supplies about 1.9 g salt per 7.5 ml (1.5 tsp): replace 250 ml beef stock with 250 ml water plus 7.5 ml concentrate and omit about 1.9 g table salt.

Commercial tourtière spice blends combine cinnamon, nutmeg, allspice, cloves, pepper, bay and savory; artisan blends are unsalted (use 10 to 15 g per 1 kg meat), while some commercial jars list sea salt first, so check the label before salting.
pitfalls: Keep seasonal sugar-shack dishes (oreilles de Christ / fried salt pork, fèves au lard) and 1950s casse-croûte fast food (poutine) distinct from everyday home cooking.

Avoid writing generic French recipes with wine reductions, tarragon cream sauces or garlic-herb butter for traditional habitant dishes where warm baking spices, summer savory, toasted flour and molasses belong.
Distinguish shallow ground-pork tourtière (pâté à la viande in Saguenay) from deep-dish Tourtière du Lac-Saint-Jean made with cubed meats, potatoes and broth.
Serve poutine with room-temperature fresh curds rather than melted mozzarella, and avoid pouring maple syrup indiscriminately into savory dishes like soupe aux pois or pâté chinois.
Quebec cretons are simmered gently with milk and oats or breadcrumbs for toast, not confited solely in lard like French rillettes.

label: Mexico
subtitle: Maize, chiles, beans, regional sauces
about: Mexico spans northern deserts, central highlands, tropical Gulf and Pacific coasts and the Yucatán Peninsula, and its food is intensely regional. Indigenous Mesoamerican systems centered on maize, beans, squash and chiles combined with ingredients and techniques introduced under Spanish colonial rule and later migrations. Tortillas, tamales, pozole and mole are representative national forms, but their ingredients and methods vary widely by region.
signature_ingredients: masa/nixtamalized maize (substitute: masa harina)
tomatillo (substitute: canned tomatillos; green tomato plus lime is only a rough fallback)
fresh and dried Mexican chiles (substitute: closest chile by heat, fruitiness and smoke)
hoja santa (substitute: none; fennel leaf plus tarragon is only a flavor approximation)
tips: Achiote paste: usually annatto with garlic, spices, acid and salt; for 10 g homemade annatto-spice paste use about 10 g commercial paste, then reduce added salt from label sodium. Prepared mole paste can replace homemade mole base only recipe-by-recipe; start about 1:1 by weight for the concentrated paste specified, then thin according to label or recipe. Commercial adobo/seasoning powders vary; use 1:1 by weight only with salt correction.
pitfalls: Do not treat cumin as the defining national Mexican spice; its prominence varies and is often exaggerated by Tex-Mex templates.
Do not assume all tortillas are flour, all food is very hot, or all moles contain chocolate.
Regional chile choices matter and are not interchangeable without changing the dish.

label: Any
subtitle: Tacos, salsa, chiles, lime
about: Outside Mexico, the internationally recognized picture centers on tacos, tortillas, salsa, guacamole, enchiladas and chile-forward sauces. That image mixes genuine Mexican national forms with restaurant exports and, especially in the United States and Europe, Tex-Mex elements such as heavy cumin, yellow cheese and hard-shell combination plates. Representative export-image dishes are tacos, enchiladas, guacamole and salsa, but the real national cuisine is far more regionally specific.
signature_ingredients: masa harina (substitute: fresh masa)
tomatillos (substitute: canned tomatillos)
Mexican dried chiles (substitute: closest named chile where possible)
queso fresco (substitute: mild feta with less salt, imperfect)
tips: Taco seasoning packets are an export shortcut, not a Mexican default: if used, replace the recipe's combined chile/cumin/garlic/onion/salt by equal weight and subtract label-derived salt. Jarred salsa can replace table salsa 1:1 by weight when convenience matters, but should not stand in for mole or a dish-specific cooked sauce.
pitfalls: Flag hard-shell tacos with ground beef, large amounts of yellow cheese and cumin-heavy packet seasoning as Tex-Mex/American export conventions rather than universal Mexican norms.
Do not call every chile sauce 'mole' or assume chocolate, sour cream and cheddar belong in all Mexican dishes.
pantry: dried or canned black or pinto beans

label: Northern & Baja
subtitle: Wheat, grilled meat, seafood, chiles
about: Northern Mexico covers arid border states such as Sonora, Chihuahua, Coahuila and Nuevo León, while Baja California is a long Pacific/Gulf peninsula with strong fishing and border-city traditions. Indigenous foodways, Spanish ranching and wheat agriculture, cattle culture, border exchange and in Baja later Asian and Mediterranean influences all matter. Carne asada, flour tortillas, machaca and cabrito are northern signatures; Baja fish tacos and seafood tostadas represent the peninsula.
signature_ingredients: large Sonoran-style flour tortillas (substitute: thin burrito-size flour tortillas)
chiltepin (substitute: pequin chile, then crushed red pepper as rough fallback)
machaca (substitute: shredded dried beef or jerky rehydrated, uncertain across brands)
fresh Pacific shellfish (substitute: locally fresh shrimp, scallops or white fish)
tips: Carne-asada seasoning: often salt, garlic, pepper, chile/cumin; use equal weight for the recipe's dry seasoning and reduce salt from label sodium. Bottled hot sauce or salsa can stand in for a simple chile-acid table sauce 1:1 by weight, but not for a cooked salsa with specific chiles.
pitfalls: Do not collapse northern Mexico into Tex-Mex: cumin and yellow cheese should not be automatic.

Northern Mexico itself is diverse, and Baja seafood is not simply 'carne asada by the sea.' The claim that flour tortillas are 'inauthentic Mexican' is wrong in northern regions, where wheat has a long history.

label: Central & Oaxacan
subtitle: Masa, moles, herbs, dried chiles
about: This node combines the central Mexican highlands with Oaxaca to the south, so it contains multiple Indigenous and mestizo cuisines rather than one style. Central markets and maize cookery connect with Oaxaca's exceptionally diverse Zapotec, Mixtec and other Indigenous traditions, alongside Afro-Mexican and Spanish influences. Tacos and tlacoyos, pozole, mole poblano, mole negro, tlayudas and memelas are representative across parts of this broad zone.
signature_ingredients: chilhuacle chiles (substitute: ancho plus pasilla; not exact)
quesillo/Oaxaca cheese (substitute: low-moisture mozzarella)
masa fresca (substitute: reconstituted masa harina)
tips: Prepared mole paste: use as the recipe's concentrated mole base by weight, commonly diluted several-fold; because brands vary greatly, follow the package ratio and treat salt/sugar as already present. Jarred salsa can replace a simple table salsa 1:1 by weight only when its chile and roast profile match.
pitfalls: Do not market Oaxaca as 'the land of seven moles' as if there were only seven; the cuisine is much more diverse.
Do not assume every mole contains chocolate or is sweet.
This combined node can hide major differences between Puebla/Mexico City/central highlands and Oaxaca, so use dish-specific chile and herb choices.
substitutes: hoja santa: no close substitute (fennel/tarragon approximation only)

label: Yucatán
subtitle: Achiote, sour orange, habanero
about: The Yucatán Peninsula sits between the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean, centered on the states of Yucatán, Campeche and Quintana Roo. Maya culinary foundations mix with Spanish colonial, Caribbean, Middle Eastern and other immigrant influences; underground pit cooking and recados are especially distinctive. Cochinita pibil, relleno negro, sopa de lima and papadzules are representative.
signature_ingredients: seville/sour orange (substitute: roughly equal parts orange and lime juice, then adjust acidity)
banana leaves (substitute: parchment plus foil for enclosure, but aroma is lost)
xcatic chile (substitute: anaheim plus a little habanero)
achiote seeds/paste (substitute: annatto powder; paprika gives color but not flavor)
tips: Commercial recado rojo/achiote paste: replace homemade recado 1:1 by weight as a starting point, then reduce salt and acid because brands vary. For sour-orange marinade, bottled naranja agria can replace fresh juice 1:1 by weight; check salt if seasoned. Check label sodium to adjust added salt (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium).
pitfalls: Do not replace achiote with generic chili powder or make cochinita simply 'spicy pulled pork.' Habanero is often served in salsa or condiment form rather than making every dish searingly hot.
Yucatecan cuisine is not merely Mexican food plus citrus; recados, Maya techniques and local herbs matter.
pantry: sour orange juice (or orange and lime)

label: Caribbean
subtitle: Scallion, thyme, chile, allspice
about: The Caribbean is an island region stretching from the Greater Antilles to the Lesser Antilles and nearby mainland-facing islands, so it contains many cuisines rather than one. Indigenous Caribbean foodways, European empires, the forced migration of Africans, indentured South Asian labor, Chinese migration and intra-Caribbean movement created overlapping but distinct traditions. Jerk, rice-and-peas dishes, roast pork, curries and plantain preparations are representative across different islands, not universal to all.
signature_ingredients: culantro/recao (substitute: cilantro, weaker and different)
Scotch bonnet (substitute: habanero)
saltfish (substitute: other salted cod)
pigeon peas/gandules (substitute: canned pigeon peas; black-eyed peas only as a texture fallback)
tips: Caribbean green seasoning and sofrito jars vary by island: use 1:1 by weight only when the product matches the target cuisine, then reduce fresh aromatics. Jerk paste can replace a homemade jerk marinade concentrate roughly 1:1 by weight; salt varies, so derive salt from label sodium.
pitfalls: Never flatten the Caribbean into 'jerk + coconut + rum.' Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, Haiti, Barbados and other islands have different colonial, linguistic and migration histories.
Use a country/island child node whenever possible.

label: Any
subtitle: Jerk, coconut, rum, tropical spice
about: Outside the region, 'Caribbean food' is often imagined as a bright tropical blend of jerk spice, coconut, rum, rice and peas, plantains, seafood and hot pepper. That shared picture borrows heavily from Jamaican and tourist-facing island cuisines and obscures major differences among Spanish-, English-, French-, Dutch- and Creole-speaking islands. Representative export-image dishes include jerk chicken, rice and peas, fried plantains and coconut-based seafood stews.
signature_ingredients: Scotch bonnet (substitute: habanero)
culantro/recao (substitute: cilantro)
green plantain (substitute: none exact)
saltfish (substitute: salted cod)
tips: Jerk seasoning or paste can shortcut only Jamaican-leaning dishes, not 'Caribbean' cuisine generally; use equal weight to the homemade paste and correct salt from sodium. Canned coconut milk can replace freshly squeezed coconut milk 1:1 by weight but may be richer; thin with water if needed.
pitfalls: This is deliberately an outsider stereotype node.
Do not apply jerk, coconut or rum to Cuban or Puerto Rican dishes automatically, and do not present 'island food' as one cuisine.
Many Caribbean cooks would object to collapsing their distinct national and ethnic traditions into this profile.
pantry: dried or canned beans or pigeon peas
Scotch bonnet or hot pepper sauce

label: Cuban
subtitle: Garlic, sour orange, cumin, oregano
about: Cuban cuisine developed on the large island of Cuba, between Florida, the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean. Taíno continuities, Spanish colonial foodways, African and Afro-Cuban traditions, Caribbean exchange and later Chinese and other migrations all contributed. Ropa vieja, lechón asado, moros y cristianos or congrí, picadillo and ajiaco are representative.
signature_ingredients: malanga (substitute: taro, closest; potato is a weaker texture substitute)
boniato (substitute: white sweet potato)
culantro (substitute: cilantro)
tips: Bottled mojo criollo can replace homemade mojo 1:1 by weight for marinade volume, but check salt and acidity; reduce salt using label sodium. Jarred sofrito can replace freshly sautéed sofrito roughly 1:1 by weight, varies widely because formulas and water content vary.
pitfalls: Do not make all Cuban food hot; chile heat is usually less central than garlic, citrus, cumin and oregano.
Do not assume the Miami Cuban sandwich is identical to all Cuban home cooking, and do not erase African or Chinese contributions by describing the cuisine as simply Spanish-Caribbean.
pantry: sour orange juice (or orange and lime)
substitutes: sour orange: orange juice plus lime juice

label: Puerto Rican
subtitle: Sofrito, adobo, achiote, culantro
about: Puerto Rican cuisine comes from the mountainous and coastal island of Puerto Rico in the Greater Antilles. Taíno ingredients and techniques, Spanish colonization, African and Afro-Puerto Rican foodways and later US influence all shaped it. Arroz con gandules, pernil, pasteles, mofongo and asopao are representative.
signature_ingredients: ají dulce (substitute: mini sweet pepper plus a tiny piece of habanero for aroma, uncertain across brands)
culantro/recao (substitute: cilantro)
gandules (substitute: canned pigeon peas)
green plantain (substitute: none for mofongo; starchy banana is not equivalent)
tips: Jarred sofrito: use about the same weight as fresh blended sofrito, then cook it out; salt content varies. Packet sazón: often salt, coriander/garlic, annatto and sometimes MSG; replace an equal weight of recipe dry seasoning only after calculating salt from label sodium. Adobo seasoning likewise needs sodium-based salt correction.
pitfalls: Do not confuse Puerto Rican sofrito with tomato-heavy Italian soffritto or assume it is the same as every Caribbean sofrito.
Do not call mofongo Dominican or Cuban by default; related mashed-plantain dishes exist elsewhere, but mofongo is strongly identified with Puerto Rico.
Heat from hot chiles is optional in much home cooking.

label: Jamaican
subtitle: Pimento, Scotch bonnet, thyme, scallion
about: Jamaican cuisine comes from the mountainous island of Jamaica in the Greater Antilles. Indigenous Taíno legacies, British colonial rule, African and Maroon foodways, and later Indian, Chinese and other migrations shaped a cuisine with strong live-fire, curry and one-pot traditions. Jerk pork or chicken, ackee and saltfish, curry goat, rice and peas and escovitch fish are representative.
signature_ingredients: ackee (substitute: none for identity; hearts of palm only mimics texture poorly)
pimento wood/leaves (substitute: allspice berries plus hardwood smoke, imperfect)
saltfish (substitute: other salted cod)
tips: Jerk paste: use roughly the same weight as a concentrated homemade jerk paste, then reduce fresh chile/scallion/thyme and salt; brands vary widely. Jamaican curry powder can replace the combined ground curry spices 1:1 by weight, but bloom it in fat and adjust salt separately if the blend is salted.
pitfalls: Do not reduce jerk to a dry 'jerk spice' of cayenne and cinnamon; pimento, Scotch bonnet, thyme, scallion and smoke are central signals.
Do not assume all Jamaican food is very hot or all curry is Indian-style; Jamaican curry powders and techniques developed locally.
Avoid calling generic barbecue 'jerk.'

label: Colombian
subtitle: Hogao, cilantro, panela, plantains
about: Stretching across the Andean cordilleras and valleys (Bogotá, Medellín, Cali, Santander), a tropical Caribbean coast, a Pacific rainforest coast, and the Orinoco plains, Colombia brings together Indigenous, Spanish, Afro-Colombian, and coastal Levantine traditions. Everyday Andean home cooking, built around a simple scallion-and-tomato hogao base (often with cumin and achiote as common additions), cilantro, panela, rice, potatoes, beans, and plantains across dishes like ajiaco santafereño, sancocho, and bandeja paisa, serves as the default baseline, while coastal cooking shifts to Caribbean coconut milk, titoté, and suero costeño or Pacific hierbas de azotea seafood stews (encocado).
sweet_only: anise seed (anís en grano, mostly sweets and warm drinks)
signature_ingredients: papa criolla small yellow potato (substitute: peeled baby Yukon Gold potatoes; simmer longer and mash a few to thicken broth)
precooked cornmeal (masarepa) (substitute: precooked white or yellow arepa cornmeal; do not swap Mexican masa harina)
queso costeño & cuajada (substitute: lightly rinsed feta mixed with queso fresco for queso costeño; drained ricotta or farmer cheese for cuajada)
suero costeño cultured coastal cream (substitute: Mexican crema or sour cream thinned slightly with buttermilk and a pinch of salt)
chillangua sawtooth coriander (substitute: culantro, or double fresh cilantro stems and leaves)
sour cassava starch (almidón de yuca agrio) (substitute: sweet tapioca starch; gives chewiness without fermented tang)
cassava & green or ripe plantains (yuca & plátano) (substitute: fresh or frozen cassava and green or black-spotted plantains)
tips: Complete condiment packets (cumin, garlic, annatto, turmeric) vary widely in salt by market: domestic Colombian packets reach about 28 g salt per 100 g (reduce table salt by about 1.4 g per 5 g tsp), whereas US-export packets are often much lower in sodium, so check the label.
Beef-rib or chicken bouillon cubes run about 54 to 56% salt by weight (about 5 to 6 g salt per 9 to 11 g cube): dissolve 1 to 2 cubes per liter of soup and omit 1 to 2 tsp table salt.
Commercial annatto color packets vary from 0 to 5% salt across brands; check the label for sodium.
pitfalls: Avoid making classic Colombian dishes chile-hot: everyday ajiaco, bandeja paisa, sancocho and sudado are mild and savory, with chile heat served on the side as raw ají.
Everyday Colombian arepas (such as arepa paisa) are thinner griddled patties eaten plain, buttered or topped with cheese rather than thick split stuffed pockets.
Avoid inserting Mexican jalapeños, chipotle, flour tortillas, tomatillos or black beans (Colombia favors cargamanto red/pinto beans or lentils and builds savory bases on scallion-and-tomato hogao).

Keep regional styles intact: do not add heavy dairy to a Pacific coconut-milk encocado, do not swap parsley or basil for guascas in ajiaco, and thicken Colombian natilla with cornstarch rather than eggs.
substitutes: guascas herb (Galinsoga parviflora): no close substitute (dried oregano, parsley and a touch of cilantro only roughly approximate ajiaco)

label: Brazilian
subtitle: Garlic, dendê, chiles, herbs
about: Brazil spans the Amazon basin, Atlantic coast, dry Northeast, central savannas and temperate South, so its cuisine is strongly regional. Indigenous food systems, Portuguese colonization, enslaved Africans and later Italian, Japanese, German, Arab and other migrations shaped different local tables. Feijoada, moqueca, acarajé, pão de queijo and churrasco are representative national or regional icons rather than a single unified style.
signature_ingredients: farinha de mandioca (substitute: coarse cassava flour; no wheat-flour equivalent for farofa)
azeite de dendê (substitute: none exact; neutral oil plus paprika only mimics color)
polvilho azedo/doce (substitute: tapioca starch, but sour starch flavor is lost)
queijo coalho (substitute: halloumi or low-moisture grilling cheese)
tips: Tempero completo: commercial garlic/onion/herb seasoning often contains substantial salt; replace equal weight of the recipe's garlic-onion-salt seasoning and subtract salt from label sodium. Bottled molho de pimenta can replace a simple chile-vinegar condiment 1:1 by weight, not fresh malagueta in cooked dishes.
pitfalls: Do not make all Brazilian food Bahian: dendê, coconut and strong malagueta are regionally important, not universal.
Do not treat feijoada as the sole national template or assume every Brazilian dish contains black beans.
Distinguish Bahian moqueca from Espírito Santo moqueca, which traditionally uses different fat and coloring choices.

label: Peruvian
subtitle: Ají, lime, cilantro, huacatay
about: Peru runs from a cold, seafood-rich Pacific coast across the Andes to the Amazon, and its cuisine reflects all three ecological zones. Indigenous Andean and coastal traditions combined with Spanish and African influences and, from the nineteenth century onward, major Chinese and Japanese migrations that helped shape chifa and Nikkei cuisines. Ceviche, lomo saltado, ají de gallina and causa are representative.
signature_ingredients: ají amarillo paste (substitute: yellow bell pepper plus habanero, rough only)
huacatay (substitute: mint plus basil/tarragon, rough only)
choclo (substitute: large-kernel frozen corn; standard sweet corn is sweeter)
cancha/chulpe corn (substitute: corn nuts only as a texture shortcut)
chuño (substitute: potato starch only for thickening, not identity)
tips: Jarred ají amarillo or ají panca paste can replace homemade chile paste 1:1 by weight if it is a plain paste; salted/acidified brands require salt/acid adjustment. Bottled sillao can replace soy sauce 1:1 by weight; note soy and wheat. Commercial anticucho paste can replace a homemade chile-garlic-vinegar marinade concentrate approximately 1:1 by weight, varies widely because formulas vary.
pitfalls: Do not describe all Peruvian food as ceviche plus hundreds of potatoes.

Chifa and Nikkei are Peruvian traditions with their own histories, not garnish-level 'Asian fusion.' Ginger is important especially in chifa/Nikkei and some ceviche styles but is not a universal everyday seasoning; annatto is less central nationally than ají amarillo/panca.
pantry: ají amarillo and ají panca pastes

label: Argentinian
subtitle: Beef, parsley, oregano, ají
about: Argentina stretches from subtropical northwestern valleys and pampas grasslands to Patagonia and the South Atlantic coast. Indigenous Andean and Guaraní traditions, Spanish colonial foodways, gaucho cattle culture and especially large Italian and other European migrations shaped modern regional cooking. Asado, empanadas, locro, milanesa and pasta are representative, with strong provincial variation.
signature_ingredients: matambre cut (substitute: flank steak, butterflied)
provoleta (substitute: thick-cut provolone suitable for grilling)
ají molido argentino (substitute: mild crushed red pepper plus paprika)
charqui (substitute: unsweetened dried beef/jerky, rehydrated)
tips: Prepared chimichurri can replace homemade chimichurri 1:1 by weight, but bottled versions may be saltier/oilier; correct salt from sodium. Empanada seasoning blends often combine paprika, cumin, oregano and chile; use equal weight for the dry spices and adjust salt if included.
pitfalls: Do not make Argentine food uniformly spicy; ají molido is often mild and hot chile is not the national default.
Do not treat chimichurri as a mandatory marinade for every steak: it is commonly a table condiment.
Northwest locro/empanadas differ markedly from Buenos Aires Italian-influenced cooking and Patagonian lamb traditions.
pantry: dried oregano and crushed red chile (ají molido)

label: Venezuelan
subtitle: Ají dulce, masarepa, papelón, queso blanco
about: Stretching from the Caribbean coast and Orinoco river basin across the grassy llanos plains to the Andean peaks around Mérida and cities like Caracas and Maracaibo, Venezuelan home cooking unites Indigenous maize and cassava traditions with Spanish, African, and later European and Caribbean influences. Everyday savory dishes usually favor gentle, aromatic warmth over chile heat, built on slow-sweated sofrito, annatto-tinted oil, unrefined cane sugar, and salty fresh white cheeses rather than heavy spices. Signature dishes range from griddled masarepa arepas and sweet corn cachapas to pabellón criollo and plantain-leaf-wrapped Christmas hallacas.
flavors: annatto seeds and infused oil (onoto / aceite onotado)
cilantro and sawtooth coriander (cilantro / culantro de monte)
capers and green olives (alcaparras y aceitunas)
lime and sour orange (limón y naranja agria)
signature_ingredients: precooked white or yellow cornmeal (harina de maíz precocida / masarepa) (substitute: none — nixtamalized masa harina behaves differently)
firm, salty aged white cheese (queso blanco llanero or queso duro) (substitute: cotija or a blend of queso fresco and feta)
soft, stretched-curd fresh cheese (queso de mano, queso telita, or queso guayanés) (substitute: fresh mozzarella or Oaxaca cheese)
ripe black-skinned and green plantains (plátanos maduros y verdes) (substitute: none — dessert bananas are too soft and lack starch)
fresh young sweet field corn kernels (jojoto, for cachapas) (substitute: fresh sweet corn kernels blended with a pinch of cornmeal)
plantain leaves (hojas de plátano, for wrapping hallacas) (substitute: banana leaves or parchment paper)
bitter cassava flatbread (casabe) (substitute: none — crisp water crackers for serving alongside only)
black turtle beans (caraotas negras) (substitute: dried black beans)
salted cultured whey condiment and clotted cream (suero y nata criolla) (substitute: salted buttermilk for suero; salted crème fraîche or thick sour cream for nata)
cassava and tropical tubers (yuca, ocumo, ñame, apio criollo) (substitute: frozen yuca and taro, parsnip, or potato for apio criollo)
raisins and sweet wine or sherry (pasas y vino dulce, for hallacas and pastel de chucho) (substitute: raisins and sweet Marsala or port)
tips: Commercial adobo seasoning blend: usually contains salt, granulated garlic, black pepper, oregano, and cumin or turmeric. Often used at 4 to 5 g (about 1 teaspoon) in place of fresh garlic and dried oregano, typically contributing roughly 1,000 to 1,450 mg sodium (about 2.5 to 3.6 g salt equivalent, using about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium), though levels vary substantially by brand (uncertain across brands — check the label and reduce added salt).

Commercial bouillon cubes or granules (cubitos): usually contain salt, monosodium glutamate, yeast extract, dehydrated onion and garlic, fat, and herbs. One 3.5 to 4 g cube is often dissolved in 250 to 500 ml liquid instead of homemade stock, typically supplying roughly 900 to 1,050 mg sodium (about 2.3 to 2.6 g salt equivalent, at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium), with wide variation across brands and low-sodium versions (uncertain across brands).

Commercial coriander-and-annatto seasoning packets (sazón): usually contain salt, monosodium glutamate, ground coriander, dehydrated garlic, and annatto for color. Often swapped in at 1 to 1.5 g (about 1/4 teaspoon) to mimic aceite onotado and garlic, typically contributing roughly 170 to 260 mg sodium per 1 to 1.5 g (about 0.4 to 0.7 g salt equivalent, at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium), though packet weights and salt ratios vary by manufacturer (uncertain across brands).

Bottled Worcestershire-style seasoning sauce (salsa inglesa): usually contains vinegar, molasses or sugar, salt, anchovies, tamarind, garlic, and spices. Used directly by weight at roughly 5 to 6 g per teaspoon (typically around 50 to 65 mg sodium, or about 0.13 to 0.16 g salt equivalent at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium) in black beans, marinades, and guisos, though regional formulations vary in salt, soy, and tamarind content (uncertain across brands).

Jarred sofrito or green aliños paste: usually contains pureed onions, sweet peppers, garlic, cilantro or culantro, vinegar, and oil with added salt. Can swap in roughly 15 to 30 g (1 to 2 tablespoons) per dish when fresh ají dulce and herbs are unavailable, though sodium varies widely by brand and commercial pastes rarely match fresh ají dulce aroma (uncertain across brands).
pitfalls: Substituting Mexican nixtamalized masa harina for precooked masarepa (harina de maíz precocida), which behaves differently and will not produce classic Venezuelan arepas or hallaca dough.
Assuming Venezuelan food is chile-hot like Mexican cuisine and adding jalapeños or habaneros instead of sweet, non-spicy aromatic ají dulce.
Conflating hallacas with Mexican tamales by omitting the plantain-leaf wrapping, annatto-tinted masa, or sweet-savory guiso garnished with olives, capers, and raisins.
Assuming Venezuelan arepas are unstuffed side cakes rather than split main-meal pockets, or substituting pinto or kidney beans for black beans (caraotas negras) in pabellón criollo.
Treating casabe as a wheat flatbread or tortilla rather than a crisp, unleavened disc made from pressed bitter cassava.
pantry: Worcestershire-style sauce (salsa inglesa) and white vinegar

label: Chilean
subtitle: Merkén, cumin, pebre, Pacific seafood
about: Stretching from the arid Atacama Desert and Andean highlands in the north, through the fertile Central Valley around Santiago and coastal ports like Valparaíso, down to the rainy Chiloé Archipelago and Patagonian steppes in the south, Chilean cuisine spans desert, valley, island, and long Pacific coastlines. It grew from Indigenous foodways (Mapuche, Aymara, Quechua, and Chono-Huilliche) fused with Spanish colonial livestock, wheat, and orchard crops, later shaped by 19th-century French fashions as well as German, British, and Italian immigration. Everyday home cooking is usually mildly spiced rather than fiery—anchored by paprika-fat bases, cumin, oregano, fresh cilantro, corn, squash, beans, and cold-water shellfish—in comforting dishes such as cazuela, pastel de choclo, porotos granados, and Chiloé's pit-steamed curanto.
flavors: sweet paprika bloomed in oil or lard (ají de color)
fresh green chili (ají verde or ají cristal)
fresh sweet basil (albahaca, classic in summer corn dishes)
stone-crushed tomato-garlic-chili table sauce (chancho en piedra)
