white or red wine vinegar and lemon juice (vinagre y limón)
sweet_only: whole or ground cinnamon (canela, in mote con huesillos, leche asada, and chancaca syrup)
whole cloves (clavo de olor, simmered in chancaca syrup and pan de pascua)
dried orange peel (cáscara de naranja, steeped in chancaca syrup and mote con huesillos)
unrefined cane sugar block (chancaca, melted into spiced syrup for sopaipillas pasadas and picarones)
aniseed (anís, in sweet pastries and aguardiente infusions)
vanilla extract or bean (vainilla, in leche asada and kuchen pastries)
signature_ingredients: starchy Chilean green corn (choclo chileno) (substitute: thawed frozen white corn or sweet corn blended with 1 tablespoon cornmeal or masa harina per cob for starch and body)
fresh shelled cranberry beans (porotos granados) (substitute: fresh or thawed cranberry/borlotti beans, or soaked dried cranberry or pinto beans)
dense orange winter squash (zapallo camote) (substitute: kabocha squash or butternut squash)
hulled wheat berries (trigo mote) (substitute: pearl barley for similar chew in savory stews, or wheat berries)
toasted whole-wheat flour (harina tostada) (substitute: whole-wheat flour dry-toasted in a skillet until nutty)
dried bull kelp (cochayuyo) (substitute: dried kombu kelp, though thinner and less chewy)
dried laver seaweed (luche) (substitute: dried wakame or unseasoned nori sheets)
sun-dried peaches (huesillos) (substitute: dried peach halves, preferably unsulfured)
Chilean abalone and pink surf clams (locos and machas) (substitute: canned abalone or tenderized conch for locos; razor clams or cherrystone clams for machas)
giant Chilean barnacles and edible sea squirt (picorocos and piure) (substitute: none)
caramelized milk spread (manjar) (substitute: canned or jarred dulce de leche)
tips: Commercial salted merkén blend: typically combines dried smoked goat's-horn chili (ají cacho de cabra), toasted coriander seed, and salt, often around 70 percent chili, 20 percent salt, and 10 percent coriander, though some commercial labels reach higher sodium levels around 15,000 to 17,500 mg sodium per 100 g (roughly 38 to 44 g salt per 100 g, based on about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium; salt percentages vary widely across producers [uncertain across brands]). Swap 10 g salt-free homemade smoked chili-coriander blend plus 2 to 4 g salt per 10 g salted merkén, or use salt-free artisanal merkén 1:1 without reducing recipe salt.

Jarred or bottled Chilean chili paste (pasta de ají verde or ají rojo): usually contains fresh chili peppers, water, salt, vinegar or acetic acid, modified cornstarch or xanthan gum, and preservatives; commercial pastes often carry about 2,200 to 3,900 mg sodium per 100 g (roughly 5.5 to 9.8 g salt per 100 g, or about 0.8 to 1.5 g salt per 15 g tablespoon; varies by producer [uncertain across brands]). Swap 15 g jarred paste for 15 g seeded fresh chili blended with a splash of vinegar and reduce added recipe salt by about 1 g.

Commercial beef or chicken bouillon cubes (caldos concentrados): usually contain salt, vegetable or palm fat, monosodium glutamate, cornstarch, sugar, dehydrated meat or poultry extract, onion and garlic powder, and herbs. Standard 10 g Chilean cubes typically supply around 1,985 to 2,360 mg sodium per cube, which is about 5.0 to 5.9 g salt per cube (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium; varies slightly by producer [uncertain across brands]). Replace 250 mL homemade stock with 250 mL water plus half a 10 g cube and omit about 2.5 to 3 g table salt.

Prepared chancaca block or bottled chancaca syrup: solid unrefined cane sugar blocks contain pure cane sugar (0 g salt) and are melted 1:1 by weight with water plus cinnamon, cloves, and orange peel; bottled ready-to-pour chancaca syrup adds water, thickeners, and sometimes preservatives (negligible salt, though amounts vary on exact trace sodium across producers). Swap 100 g block chancaca for 100 g dark brown sugar or piloncillo with a small pinch of molasses.
pitfalls: Making Chilean dishes fiery like Mexican or Peruvian cooking, when everyday savory recipes usually rely on mild paprika-fat bases (ají de color) and serve heat on the side as pebre or merkén.
Substituting Peruvian ají panca paste for Chilean ají de color, which is mild sweet paprika bloomed in oil or lard rather than a smoky dried Peruvian chili.
Treating starchy Chilean choclo as interchangeable with sugary US sweet corn without adding a starch binder in pastel de choclo or humitas, which otherwise turn watery.
Adding sweet baking spices like cinnamon or cloves to savory beef pino, or assuming raisins are universally accepted in empanadas de pino despite ongoing home-cook debate.
Treating Central Valley dishes as the whole cuisine while overlooking Andean northern stews (calapurca, patasca), Chiloé's curanto and seaweeds, and Patagonian spit-roasted lamb.

label: The Guianas
subtitle: Cassareep, masala, kecap manis, culantro
about: The Guianas lie on the Atlantic shoulder of northeastern South America, where low coastal plains, tidal mudflats, and broad rivers—the Essequibo, Demerara, Suriname, and Maroni—give way inland to dense Amazonian rainforest and interior highlands around Georgetown, Paramaribo, and Cayenne. Indigenous cassava traditions fused with enslaved West African and Maroon foodways, British, Dutch, and French colonial larders, Sephardic Jewish baking in Suriname, and 19th- to 20th-century migrations from India, Java, China, and Laos. Home cooking balances bittersweet cassava reductions, fresh herb-and-chile seasonings, roasted-spice curries, sweet-soy stir-fries, and toasted-cassava sides, seen in Guyanese pepperpot, Surinamese pom and bami, and French Guianese bouillon d'awara.
flavors: hot chile (wiri wiri, Madame Jeanette, piment)
masala curry or colombo blend (masala / poudre de colombo)
sweet soy sauce (kecap manis / zoete ketjap)
lime and sour orange (citron vert / zure oranje)
west Indian bay leaf, cinnamon, and clove (bois d'Inde)
signature_ingredients: cassareep (substitute: none exact; dark unsweetened molasses simmered with warm spices approximates color and bittersweetness without bitter-cassava savoriness)
toasted fermented cassava semolina / couac (substitute: toasted Brazilian farinha de mandioca)
pomtayer / arrowleaf elephant ear corm (pomtajer) (substitute: malanga or yautia; taro is a softer texture fallback)
awara palm fruit pulp (pate d'awara) (substitute: none exact; West African red palm fruit concentrate approximates richness but differs in aroma)
salted cod and cured salted meats (bakkeljauw / morue / zoutvlees) (substitute: soaked dried salt cod for fish; smoked pork hock or salt pork for cured meats)
yardlong beans (kousenband / bora) (substitute: Chinese long beans or tender green beans)
bilimbi / sour tropical fruit (birambi) (substitute: unripe green mango or tamarind pulp for souring curries and chutneys)
tips: Jarred Caribbean green seasoning usually blends scallions, culantro or cilantro, thyme, garlic, onion, hot pepper, vinegar, and salt; swap roughly 1:1 by weight for fresh green seasoning and check the label, as commercial jars often supply roughly 4.5 to 8.7 g salt per 100 g (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium) whereas homemade blends are unsalted (uncertain across brands on exact brand salt levels).

Commercial bouillon cubes are widely used in Surinamese and Guyanese home cooking and usually combine salt, yeast extract or hydrolyzed protein, fat, and dried herbs; one ~4.8 g cube typically supplies roughly 2.5 to 2.9 g salt (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium), so dissolve 1 cube per 240 to 480 ml water in place of stock and sharply reduce added salt.

Dry masala and colombo powders are typically salt-free spice blends (swap 1:1 by weight for homemade spice mix), whereas jarred masala, Javanese bumbu, and peanut or chili sambal pastes add oil, aromatics, sugar, shrimp paste, and salt; swap jarred pastes roughly 1:1 by weight for freshly ground paste and adjust salt from the label (roughly 0.8 to 2.5 g salt per 100 g at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium, though amounts vary due to wide brand variation).

Commercial sweet soy sauce (kecap manis) usually supplies roughly 3.5 to 3.7 g salt per 100 g (about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium), so reduce added salt in stir-fries and marinades; traditional pure bottled cassareep contains no added salt, though some commercial bottles add sugar, caramel coloring, or preservatives (check labels and reduce added brown sugar if sweetened, though amounts vary if soy extract is added).
pitfalls: Do not flatten the Guianas into generic island Caribbean 'jerk and coconut' cooking or assume Spanish-speaking Latin American profiles apply.

Do not treat the three territories as interchangeable: Guyana centers Indo-Guyanese and Afro-Creole dishes with cassareep, Suriname adds major Javanese, Hindustani, and Sephardic-Creole traditions, and French Guiana leans Franco-Antillean and Amazonian Creole.
Never suggest using raw or under-boiled bitter cassava root or juice in home recipes, as un-detoxified bitter cassava contains toxic cyanogenic glycosides.
Do not swap sweet soy sauce (kecap manis) and cassareep interchangeably: both are dark and thick, but kecap manis is salty-sweet fermented soy while cassareep is an unsalted bitter-cassava reduction.

Do not confuse Surinamese masala or French Guianese colombo powder with generic US curry powder, as colombo includes toasted rice and warm cloves while Guianas masalas emphasize roasted cumin and fenugreek.
pantry: neutral cooking oil and coconut oil
dried yellow split peas and black-eyed peas
hot chiles (wiri wiri, Madame Jeanette, or habanero)
limes and cane or white vinegar
masala or curry powder and ground cumin (geera)
sweet soy sauce (kecap manis) and cassareep
